ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating 5.0 GW of wind power, with Scottish wind contributing an estimated 2.4 GW, representing 23.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Scotland’s electricity grid is operating at a remarkably clean carbon intensity of just 5 gCO2/kWh, compared to the GB-wide intensity of 203 gCO2/kWh. However, structural cross-border transmission limits prevent this clean electricity from flowing south to major demand centres. Consequently, 14.5 GWh of Scottish generation has been turned down so far today through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a direct constraint cost of £597,411. To replace this curtailed renewable volume, fossil-fuel plants elsewhere in Britain had to burn an estimated 2,748,787 m3 of natural gas, emitting an avoidable 5,064 tonnes of CO2. Annualised at this daily run rate, the total yearly cost of curtailment would reach approximately £218 million, which increases consumer bills across the UK by an estimated £1/MWh on final electricity invoices. This stark divergence highlights a persistent operational barrier: abundant zero-carbon power is being wasted at significant consumer and environmental expense, reinforcing the critical necessity of accelerated grid transmission expansion and strategic deployment of long-duration energy storage.
